what_it_does: Event-based cameras are a new kind of image sensor that, instead of capturing full frames at fixed intervals, fire a tiny signal each time a single pixel detects a change in brightness — so fast-moving objects produce a sparse stream of timestamped dots rather than blurry frames. The problem is that these cameras tend to have low spatial resolution, so fine details are lost. This paper proposes a chip design that runs a spiking neural network (a brain-inspired computing model where artificial neurons fire pulses rather than computing smooth numbers) to reconstruct a higher-resolution event stream directly on the sensor chip, without shipping raw data off to a server. The key hardware trick is a new way of organizing the computation — called KCTR (Kernel-Channel-Timestamp-Row) dataflow — that lets two processing stages run in parallel through the same hardware, eliminating the need to store intermediate spike results in a large off-chip memory buffer. The result is a more compact and power-efficient architecture for in-camera, real-time event super-resolution.
